Your hesitation is actually the smart instinct talking, and here's why it makes sense.

"The main way people use it is on their phone" and "I need an Apple Developer account" are two different things. It's easy to blur them together, but they're not the same decision.

Right now Haven is a PWA. That means someone on their iPhone can open it in Safari, tap Share, then "Add to Home Screen," and it runs full-screen with your icon like a real app. No App Store. No $99/year. No review process. You already built the manifest and the maskable icons for exactly this. So the phone experience you care about most, you already have it, for free, today.

What the Apple Developer account actually buys you is App Store distribution specifically. That's a separate layer:

- A listing people can search and download from the App Store
- The trust signal of "it's a real app in the store"
- A few native-only capabilities (though iOS PWAs now do web push, home screen, offline, most of what you'd want early)

The reason your gut is holding back: none of that matters yet. You're at the waitlist stage. Your job right now is to find out if people want the thing, not to get it listed in a store. The $99/year, the review cycles, the build tooling (you'd likely need something like Capacitor or a rewrite to wrap the web app) are all real cost and real time, and they don't move the needle on "do people want Haven."

So the honest framing: you're not hesitant because you're avoiding the main thing. You're hesitant because part of you knows the App Store isn't the main thing yet. The main thing is the phone experience, and the PWA already delivers that.

My recommendation: skip the Apple Developer account for now. Make the PWA install flow feel great on iPhone (that's the real lever), get people using it, and revisit the App Store only when you have signal that distribution or a native capability is the actual bottleneck.

This is a great brain-dump, and there's a real product in here. Let me separate the parts, because the native-vs-PWA decision only hangs on one of them, and it's not the one you think.

## First, name the core

Strip everything back and Haven is one thing: a searchable private memory network. You know things about people (where they work, where you met them, the Spain shirt at Katrin, how to reach them), and today that knowledge is scattered and unsearchable. Haven makes it searchable. "Who do I know at LinkedIn in SF" and it answers. That's the product. That's the wedge.

Everything else you described (bump-to-sync, ambient auto-detect, Love Alarm) is a way to *feed* that network. They're input mechanisms, not the product. Important distinction, because it tells you what to protect and what to defer.

## The key insight you already have

You nailed it: input is the hardest thing. And you split it correctly into three layers:

1. Static data (LinkedIn/IG/X-scrapeable, plus what the user types)
2. Scraped/enriched data (feed it a link, pull more)
3. Dynamic memory data (the Spain shirt, the Amazon research team - only a human can put this in)

Here's the thing none of these three layers needs native for. A database, a good search, a clean mobile form for dumping memories. That's web. That's a PWA. The hardest and most valuable part of your app - the searchable memory - has zero dependency on the App Store.

## Now the friction you're actually worried about

You're conflating two different frictions:

**Friction A: connecting two people.** Today: open Safari, find the app, search a profile, request. Slow, ugly.

**Friction B: capturing what you remember.** The dynamic layer.

For Friction A, you do NOT need proximity magic and you do NOT need native. The boring, works-everywhere answer is a QR code. You open Haven, it shows your code, the other person scans it, connected. One second. No typing, no searching, no username-that-might-change problem. It works in a PWA today, and it works even if the other person doesn't have Haven yet (you just save them as a contact). That last part matters enormously at your stage, which I'll get to.

QR is the practical version of the NameDrop bump. It gets you 90% of the "no friction" feeling without a single native line.

## The honest read on the proximity dream

Now the fun part, and I have to be straight with you because you're about to make an infrastructure decision partly based on it.

**The NameDrop head-to-head bump:** that's Apple's own feature, using ultra-wideband and NFC. Third-party apps cannot hook into it. You can't make your app do the NameDrop motion. Even native, that door is closed. QR is your substitute.

**The Love Alarm ambient auto-detect:** this is the one feature in your whole rant that genuinely requires native. And I need you to hear the second half of that sentence: even native, on iOS, it barely works.

Here's why. Ambient detection needs Bluetooth Low Energy, both phones broadcasting an ID and scanning for others, continuously, in the background.

- On iOS, a PWA can't touch Bluetooth at all. Safari doesn't support Web Bluetooth, period. So yes, for this one feature, PWA is a hard no.
- But native iOS *also* cripples background Bluetooth. When your app is backgrounded, iOS hides the advertising data in an "overflow" area, and two backgrounded iPhones trying to detect each other is famously unreliable. "Always on, always detecting everyone around me" is not a thing iOS lets you do cleanly. It also nukes battery, and iOS will throttle you.
- Bitchat works because it's mostly foreground mesh chat, and even it fights range and reliability problems. It proves BLE mesh is *possible*, not that seamless always-on stranger-detection is *reliable*.

So the ambient feature is not "native unlocks it." It's "native gives you a shot at a hard, flaky, battery-hungry, privacy-loaded feature that even well-funded teams struggle with."

## And the network problem that kills it early anyway

Ambient detection and bump-sync both only work if the *other* person already has Haven. At MVP, with a waitlist of early users, almost nobody in the room with you has it. So these features are dead weight until you have density.

QR-to-connect and the memory network both give value when you're the *only* Haven user in the room. You can save and search people who've never heard of the app. That's single-player value, and single-player value is what lets a network app survive before it has a network.

## So, the actual answer to your hesitation

You're hesitant about the Apple Developer account because some part of you senses the truth: the App Store and native are gated to a feature (ambient proximity) that is (a) the hardest to build, (b) unreliable even when built, (c) useless until you have user density, and (d) not the core of the product anyway.

The core - searchable memory + frictionless QR connect - ships as a web app / PWA right now, for free, and is the thing that proves whether anyone wants Haven.

My recommendation:

- Build the searchable memory network and QR connect as a PWA. That's your MVP.
- Get people using it, prove the "who do I know at X in Y" magic and the memory recall actually delights.
- File ambient proximity under "v3 moonshot." Revisit native only when you have (1) proof people love the core and (2) enough local density that proximity would even fire.
- When that day comes, going native is a known path (wrap the web app with Capacitor, or build a thin native shell), and $99/year will feel obvious instead of scary.

Don't let the coolest, hardest, least-proven feature drag your whole stack native before the boring valuable core has earned it.

Good, a decision. The $99 is a rounding error compared to the time you're about to spend either way, and "I keep hesitating" was costing more than the money. Let's make the native path smart instead of just committed. Point by point:

## 1. Social data as matching fuel

The instinct is right and the shape is right: opt-in, machine-only access, abstract matches ("A also likes soccer, want to check them out?") that reveal interest overlap without leaking the underlying data. That's genuinely the correct privacy architecture for this kind of matching.

Two honest cautions:

- "No human can ever see it" is an engineering promise, not a settings toggle. If you ever say that publicly, it has to be backed by real architecture (encryption at rest, no admin read paths, audited access). Don't say it before it's true, because it's the kind of promise that kills trust permanently if broken.
- "The system reads my texts and auto-suggests people" is a v4 idea sitting on top of a v1 that doesn't exist yet. File it in the vision doc. Its real value today is as a design constraint: build the data model now so every piece of profile/memory data is a searchable, permissioned data point. Then matching later is a feature, not a rearchitecture.

## 2. Reducing the "open the app" friction

Yes, this is exactly what native buys you, and it's more boring and more real than the Love Alarm stuff:

- Lock screen / Home Screen widget: tap, QR is on screen in under a second. Fully supported, reliable, shippable.
- Control Center widget and the Action button on newer iPhones can deep-link straight to your QR screen too.
- App Clips are the underrated one: the other person scans your QR and gets a lightweight slice of Haven instantly without installing the full app. That attacks the "the other person doesn't have Haven" problem, which is your actual biggest friction.
- NameDrop's head-to-head motion stays closed to third parties. That one's Apple-only, native or not. QR + widget gets you functionally the same speed.

So the frictionless connect story is: widget -> QR -> App Clip. Every piece of that is supported, stable iOS API. No fighting the OS.

## 3. Calendar-based event inference

This is the best new idea in this message. "You connected at 4pm, your calendar had a 3-5pm event, so we pre-fill 'met at X' and you confirm or edit" is exactly how dynamic data capture should work: the machine drafts, the human confirms. It turns your hardest input problem (nobody writes notes) into a one-tap confirmation.

And note: this one doesn't even need native. Google Calendar OAuth works on web, and native later gets you Apple Calendar via EventKit as a bonus. Timestamp of connection + calendar lookup + editable pre-fill. Cheap to build, high value. This should be in the MVP.

LinkedIn-as-the-static-source: right scope. One scrape target, connect = mutual searchability. Keep it that narrow.

## 4. Ambient detection: channel the confidence into the version that works

I respect the "if it's possible we'll figure it out" energy, and I won't tell you not to try. But let me redirect it, because there's a version of this feature that is reliable today and it's not the one you described:

**Foreground radar mode.** You're at an event, you open Haven, hit "radar on," phone can stay in your pocket with the app open or recently active. BLE advertising and scanning in the foreground works well. The 3-5m / 5min dwell heuristic, the queue, the swipe-at-home review: all of that works in this mode. This is the "do things that don't scale" version, and it maps to real behavior anyway: people know when they're at a networking event.

**Background always-on** is where iOS actively fights you, and here's the part that matters: it's not a puzzle with a clean solution nobody found yet. Apple deliberately restricts it, and the apps that pushed hardest (all the COVID contact-tracing apps) only worked because Apple built them a special OS-level API that you cannot use. That's the strongest possible evidence about where the ceiling is. iOS moves backgrounded BLE advertising into an overflow area that other backgrounded iPhones can't scan, and no amount of cleverness changes what the radio broadcasts.

So: ship radar as an explicit event mode first. If it turns out people love it, you'll have the usage data (and maybe by then the platform reality) to justify grinding on background mode. Starting with the background fight means burning months on the least reliable piece before anyone has ever swiped through a queue.

Requiring a profile at signup for sync to work: yes, obviously fine. That's not friction, that's the product.

## 5 and 6. Agreed, and agreed

Input is the whole game, and your current manual entry is the brute-force placeholder for it. And the $99: do it today so the account review clock (it can take a day or two) starts running while you build.

## What I'd actually do, in order

1. Register the Apple Developer account now.
2. Keep building the core as the web app it already is: searchable profiles, QR connect, LinkedIn scrape, calendar-inferred event tagging. All of this ships regardless of packaging.
3. Wrap it native with Capacitor (your React + Convex app drops in mostly as-is) rather than rewriting. Native shell gives you the widget, App Clip, EventKit, and BLE plugins when you're ready.
4. Widget + QR + App Clip = the frictionless connect story.
5. Radar as foreground event mode, later.

An App Clip is a tiny slice of Haven - under ~15MB - that launches instantly when someone scans your QR or taps an NFC tag. No App Store trip, no install, it just opens and runs. Apple built it for exactly the "let a stranger use one feature right now" moment.

So the flow: you show your QR, the other person (who has never heard of Haven) scans it, an App Clip opens showing "this is Tony, connect back / save his contact." They do the one thing. Then the App Clip nudges them: "get Haven to keep your own network." They can even sign in with Apple inside the clip, so it's not a cold wall.

The difference from the full app:

- App Clip is ephemeral. iOS cleans it up, it has limited storage, no home screen presence, no widget, no notifications, no persistent account of their own.
- The full app is where they get *their own searchable network*. The clip lets them receive; the app lets them own.

So: does a person need to install and sign up to use it? To be *received into your network* and connect back in the moment - no, the clip handles that with minimal friction. To have their own directory, their own memories, their own searchable people - yes, they install and make a profile.

What makes someone install: the clip gives them a taste (someone just connected with me effortlessly), and the app gives them the actual product (I can now store and search everyone *I* know). The clip is the hook; the search is the reason to stay. This is your answer to the two-sided cold-start problem - a non-user experiences Haven the first time without the install wall, in the exact moment connection is valuable.

## 5. Calendar as add-on, not core

Agreed, and you reasoned it correctly. Core = store + search. Calendar inference is a magic-moment enhancer for the memory layer, not a requirement to prove the core. Ship the core, watch whether people even fill in "where we met," and if that's the friction point, calendar inference becomes the obvious unlock. Testing tells you. Park it.

## 6. Going native - one reassurance so you don't waste months

"Focus native because no one opens a web URL" is a fair read of user behavior. But hear this clearly: **native does not mean rewrite.** Your current React + Convex app becomes the native app by wrapping it with Capacitor. Your existing code runs inside a real App Store app that gets a real icon, the widget, App Clips, NFC, Bluetooth plugins, all of it. You are not throwing away what you've built - you're putting a native shell around it and stopping promoting the bare URL.

That matters for your money and time: the $99 and the App Store listing are the packaging. The React/Convex directory you already have is the product inside. Same codebase, native delivery.

## 7. What the COVID contact-tracing apps were

During 2020-2021, governments built phone apps to detect whether you'd recently been physically near someone who later tested positive - using Bluetooth proximity between phones. That is *precisely* Haven's radar problem: detect which other phones were close to yours.

They ran straight into the wall I described. Background Bluetooth on iOS was too unreliable and drained too much battery to work. So Apple and Google did something they almost never do: they jointly built a special OS-level system (the Exposure Notification API) that let phones swap rotating anonymous Bluetooth IDs in the background, reliably and low-power. It solved the exact problem.

But they locked it down: one app per country, public health authorities only, COVID only. Regular developers cannot touch it.

The lesson for you: the most resourced, government-backed, Apple-cooperative attempt at this exact feature could only work because Apple built a private API - and then walled it off from everyone else. It's not that nobody has cracked background BLE proximity. Apple cracked it, and won't hand you the key. That's the ceiling, and it's why radar is a "future, if ever" item, not an MVP gate.

## 8. Cloud + satellite (GPS) instead of Bluetooth - would that work?

Good question, and it's a genuinely different architecture, so let me be precise. "Satellite" here means GPS: the phone reads its own location, reports it to your cloud, and your server compares two Haven users' locations to see if they're near each other. This is how Snap Map and Find My Friends work.

Does it dodge the Bluetooth wall? Yes - no OS radio restriction. But it trades that problem for two others:

- **Precision.** GPS is good to about 5-20 meters outdoors on a good day, and much worse or useless indoors - which is exactly where you network: bars, conference halls, event rooms. GPS cannot reliably tell "these two people are 3 meters apart having a conversation" from "10 meters apart ignoring each other across the room." Your whole radar concept depends on that 3-5m dwell distinction, and GPS can't deliver it indoors.
- **Privacy and battery.** Continuously uploading everyone's precise location to your server, in the background, is a far bigger privacy and legal surface than Bluetooth, which can stay on-device. "Always" background location is also battery-heavy and gets heavy scrutiny in App Store review. It's the category of thing that draws regulators.

So GPS-cloud is *easier to build reliably* than background BLE, but *not precise enough* for the "who did I actually talk to" use case, and *more* privacy-loaded. Net: it doesn't rescue the radar feature. Which is fine, because you already put radar in the "future, not now" bucket. That was the right call.

---

So where you've landed, and I agree with all of it:

- MVP: centralized context store + AI-searchable directory. Web codebase, delivered as a native app via Capacitor.
- Frictionless connect: widget -> QR -> App Clip. All native, all reliable, all shippable.
- LinkedIn scrape: needed for the search baseline (point 2 of your core), not for basic referencing. Add when you build search-by-attribute.
- Calendar inference and ambient radar: parked as future, validated by usage.

Want me to scope the Capacitor wrap against this actual codebase next - what it touches, what the widget and App Clip need - or start on the QR connect flow, since it's pure web and unblocks the whole "add a person in one second" story?

Let us look at what is true, what is false, and what is uncertain about creating Love Alarm style device detection today.

What is true: A purely software based app running on two standard smartphones in their pockets, scanning and advertising continuously with high precision in the background, is blocked by Apple and Google operating system architecture. You cannot write standard iOS code that turns a locked phone into a continuous background Bluetooth beacon for other phones without the OS throttling or killing it.

What is false: The idea that background phone to phone Bluetooth is the only way to create the Love Alarm experience.

What is uncertain: Whether your initial users actually care about passive continuous background scanning, or if they just care about the emotional moment when someone who matches them is nearby.

If you are committed to making this exist, you essentially have three different paths to invent around the platform wall. Each path forces a radically different trade off on your startup.

First, you can invent around the software by building physical hardware. If phones refuse to advertise reliably in the background, a dedicated wearable like a smart pin, ring, or keyfob will advertise continuously without operating system restrictions. The phone then acts as the receiver, or the tokens communicate directly. This bypasses Apple background advertising rules entirely. But ask yourself: Are you ready to take on hardware manufacturing, distribution, and unit economics just to test if people want the social experience?

Second, you can use hybrid system capabilities. You can combine background location triggers with server side distance calculations, or leverage active system states like Live Activities to keep spatial scanning alive when a user enters a social venue. It gives you room level proximity rather than exact sub meter Bluetooth precision, but it works on existing devices today. Is exact ten meter precision mandatory for the core user emotion, or is knowing you are both in the same coffee shop enough?

Third, you can invent a new interaction ritual. Love Alarm in the drama relied on passive scanning, but what if the magic comes from active intent? What if users tap an activate radar button when they step into a bar, triggering a short, high precision scanning window while the app is active?

As a founder, your biggest risk right now is not whether Bluetooth physics can be hacked. Your biggest risk is spending six months inventing a complex technical bypass before proving that users actually want the core social outcome.

Which part of the problem are you most eager to invent: the hardware, the software workaround, or the user experience itself? and gpt: Yes—but the invention needs to happen around iOS, not by somehow defeating it.
You can build something that feels like Love Alarm. The difficult version is:
Detect every Haven user within roughly 10 meters, instantly, while both phones are locked and the app has not been opened recently.
A normal iPhone app cannot promise that. iOS allows background Bluetooth modes, but background advertisements are reduced, discoveries are combined, and scan intervals become longer. Apple describes Bluetooth advertising as “best effort.” (Apple Developer)
But there are several versions you can build.
1. The realistic phone-only Haven MVP
Create an intentional Radar Mode:
    1    The user activates “Visible for the next 15 minutes.”
    2    Haven advertises a common Bluetooth service identifier.
    3    Nearby Haven phones scan for that identifier.
    4    After discovering each other, they exchange rotating anonymous IDs.
    5    Your server determines whether there is a relevant connection.
    6    The phone produces the alarm animation, vibration, or notification.
When both apps are foregrounded—or at least actively being used—this can work well. Apple’s Multipeer Connectivity framework is specifically designed to discover and communicate with nearby instances of an app using Bluetooth and peer-to-peer networking. (Apple Developer)
You could design it around moments where users naturally activate it:
    •    Entering an event
    •    Walking into a café
    •    Attending a conference
    •    Joining a university social space
    •    Starting “available to meet” mode
That is still a real Love Alarm experience. It just is not secretly operating with perfect reliability every second of the day.
2. The hybrid version I would build first
Do not make Bluetooth responsible for the entire system.
Use several increasingly precise signals:
Same city
   ↓
Same venue or geographic zone
   ↓
Both users currently active
   ↓
Bluetooth encounter detected
   ↓
Sustained strong Bluetooth signal
   ↓
Trigger Haven alarm
Location or venue participation narrows the candidates. Bluetooth confirms that two devices were likely physically close. This avoids continuously searching for every phone in the world.
For example, at a startup event:
    1    Tony joins the event’s Haven room.
    2    Twenty other people join.
    3    The backend knows those users might be nearby.
    4    Radar Mode only looks for anonymous IDs belonging to that room.
    5    When a relevant ID remains nearby for several seconds, Haven triggers.
This architecture also makes false-positive prevention, privacy controls, blocking, and consent much easier.
3. The actual invention: a Haven wearable
If you want continuous, dependable detection, create a small physical device:
    •    A pin
    •    Bracelet
    •    Keychain
    •    Card
    •    Ring
    •    Clip attached to a phone case
Each Haven Beacon would:
    1    Continuously broadcast rotating anonymous Bluetooth IDs.
    2    Continuously listen for other Haven Beacons.
    3    Measure approximate signal strength.
    4    Record encounters locally.
    5    Vibrate or glow immediately when conditions match.
    6    Synchronize encounter data with the Haven app later.
Haven Beacon A  ← Bluetooth →  Haven Beacon B
       ↓                              ↓
   iPhone A                        iPhone B
       ↓                              ↓
                  Haven backend
The crucial difference is that your hardware controls its background execution. Apple cannot suspend the beacon’s processor the way it suspends an iPhone app.
A prototype could be made with an inexpensive low-power Bluetooth microcontroller. After proving the experience, you could investigate UWB for more accurate ranging. Apple officially supports interactions between iPhones and third-party UWB accessories through Nearby Interaction, although developing compatible accessories involves Apple’s accessory specifications and approved hardware solutions. (Apple Developer)
However, Apple’s phone-to-phone Nearby Interaction is not itself passive stranger discovery: the apps must first exchange discovery tokens, and Apple describes the distance-and-direction interaction as running while the app is in the foreground. (Apple Developer)
What I would not attempt
I would not rely on:
    •    Playing silent audio to keep Haven alive
    •    Pretending to be a navigation or fitness app
    •    Abusing VoIP background execution
    •    Keeping the microphone continuously active for ultrasound
    •    Wi-Fi MAC-address tracking
    •    Trying to use Find My as a general nearby-user network
These would be unreliable, privacy-sensitive, or likely to create App Store review problems. Apple explicitly says background services may only be used for their intended purposes. (Apple Developer)
The strongest path for Haven
Build it in stages:
Stage 1 — Active Radar
Phone-only, opt-in, app open, rotating IDs, Bluetooth scanning. Test whether people actually enjoy the alarm moment.
Stage 2 — Social spaces
Event rooms, café zones, campus areas, parties and conferences. Use check-in plus Bluetooth confirmation.
Stage 3 — Imperfect background encounters
Experiment with legitimate Core Bluetooth background modes. Treat detections as opportunistic—not guaranteed—and never promise instant detection.
Stage 4 — Haven Beacon
Only after proving demand, develop a wearable that performs continuous proximity detection independently of the phone.
So yes, you can make Love Alarm. The first product should not be “magically detect everyone everywhere.” It should be:
Turn on Haven Radar and discover when a meaningful person is physically near you.
Then, if that moment is valuable enough, the hardware becomes the invention that removes Apple’s ceiling.

You are advising a solo founder on architecture decisions for their app "Haven." Give a direct, opinionated recommendation, not a survey. This is a strategy/advice question - do NOT write or change any code, do NOT explore the filesystem. Just reason and recommend based on the context below.

## The app
Haven is, at its core, a "searchable private memory network" / personal AI directory of the people you know. You save people (name, socials, where they work, where you met them, freeform memories like "met at a party, wore a Spain shirt, works at Amazon research"), and later you search by any attribute: "who do I know who works at LinkedIn and lives in SF?" or "who was the person I met at the bar wearing a Spain shirt?" Two of the core value props are (1) a centralized contact hub, and (2) attribute-based people search that normal platforms (LinkedIn/IG) don't offer. Later features: LinkedIn scraping to enrich profiles, semantic/AI search over people and memories, matching people by shared interests.

## Current stack
- Frontend: React (Vite), currently shipped as a PWA
- Backend: Convex (reactive backend, has document DB, full-text search indexes, and vector search / embeddings built in)
- Auth: Clerk
- Solo founder, pre-launch (waitlist stage), MVP not built yet
- They have decided to go native iOS (registered/registering Apple Developer account) because "nobody opens a web URL" - the phone is the primary surface.

## The two decisions they're asking about

DECISION 1: Native packaging.
Should they REWRITE the iOS app natively in Swift, or WRAP their existing React + Convex codebase with Capacitor (WKWebView shell + native plugins for widgets, App Clips, Bluetooth, EventKit)? Consider: solo founder, MVP stage, existing React codebase, need for native capabilities later (Home Screen widget for QR, App Clip for frictionless connect, possibly Bluetooth "radar" much later, calendar access). Weigh dev velocity, maintainability, the cost of throwing away working code, and whether Capacitor's limitations would actually block any of their planned features.

DECISION 2: Datastore for the searchable directory.
The founder believes "Postgres is better for searching." Options they're weighing:
  (a) Migrate entirely from Convex to Postgres
  (b) Keep Convex for one kind of data (user management) and use Postgres for the "network"/searchable people data
  (c) Just use one datastore
Consider what Convex actually offers for search: full-text search indexes and native vector search (for embeddings/semantic search over people and memories). Consider what Postgres offers: pg_trgm fuzzy matching, tsvector full-text, pgvector, rich multi-attribute filtering and joins. Consider the real cost of a hybrid two-datastore setup for a SOLO founder pre-launch (data sync, consistency, two mental models, two sets of ops). Consider that their search needs at MVP are: filter people by structured attributes (company, city, role) + eventually semantic search over freeform memories.

## What I want from you
For each decision: a clear recommendation, the 2-3 reasons that actually drive it, and the main risk of your recommendation. Be concrete and practical for a solo founder who needs to ship and validate, not build a perfect system. Keep it tight - a few hundred words total. Plain ASCII only, no em dashes, no emoji. Your entire response is returned to the orchestrator to relay, so make it self-contained.

content.text:
## 1. The QR / connection question - the unlock

Here's the sentence that dissolves your confusion: **connecting is a data exchange, and for B to save A, A must supply some data. That's not an iOS limitation - it's just how information works.** There is no magic where B's phone learns about A when A carries zero data. So the real question is never "can we avoid A supplying data," it's "how low can we push the friction of A supplying it."

That reframes your two cases into three friction tiers:

**Tier 1 - both have Haven (your case 1).** A scans B's QR, taps connect, done. Both profiles already exist, so both directories get populated instantly and mutually. Zero typing. This is the dream case and it's clean. And notice: the scan itself IS the consent. You physically met and chose to scan, so you don't need the old "send request -> other accepts" dance. Auto-connect on scan is legitimate and it's a real friction win over LinkedIn. Keep that.

**Tier 2 - A has no Haven, B does (your case 2).** This is where you got stuck, and you're right that plain QR "leads nowhere" for B. A scans B's QR, A sees B's card (good for A), but B gets nothing because A has no profile to send back. The fix is the App Clip, and specifically an App Clip with a "connect back" step:

- A scans B's QR -> App Clip opens on A's phone (no install) -> shows B's card -> button: "Connect back."
- A taps it -> Sign in with Apple, which autofills A's name in one tap -> a lightweight Haven identity is created for A right there.
- Now A has minimal data, so B receives A's card. Mutual connection achieved, and A never left the moment or visited an app store.

So App Clip does NOT only work when A already has an account - that's the misconception. App Clip's whole reason to exist is to pull a non-user into a minimal identity in the moment, without the install wall. A can upgrade to the full app later. The key detail: **the person WITHOUT the app scans the person WITH the app's QR**, because the QR launches the App Clip on the non-user's phone.

**Tier 3 - A refuses everything, or you're offline / no App Clip.** Fallback: B manually types A in. This is exactly your current brute-force manual entry. It never goes away entirely, it's just the floor you land on when Tiers 1 and 2 don't apply.

So your diagram's case 2 resolves to: A scans -> App Clip shows B's card AND offers connect-back-with-Apple -> one tap -> both saved. Design the App Clip and case 2 stops being "damn that's a lot of friction" and becomes "one extra tap for the person who hasn't joined yet." That one tap is also your best user-acquisition moment, because A just felt Haven work before installing anything.

One more: who owns the QR. Simplest model is every user has one personal, permanent QR (their card). It can live on a Home Screen widget or Lock Screen widget - tap, QR is up in under a second. That's the native win you already spotted, and you're right that LinkedIn has no widget, so it's a real edge.

## 4. Snap Map battery, and the three-model convergence

How Snap Map avoids draining your battery: **it doesn't track continuously.** It updates your location mostly when you open Snapchat (foreground), plus sparse background updates using coarse, low-power location events. That's why a friend's Snap Map pin can be hours stale - it's opportunistic, not real-time. The trick to not nuking battery is exactly that: update on natural app-open moments and coarse background pings, never continuous high-frequency GPS. So "always-on precise" is the battery killer; "opportunistic and coarse" is the sustainable version, and even Snap chose coarse.

Now the useful thing about the Gemini and GPT answers you pasted: notice that three independent models - me, Gemini, and GPT - all landed on the exact same staged shape without coordinating:

1. Active/Radar Mode first: foreground, opt-in, "I'm visible for 15 min," triggered when you enter an event. Reliable today.
2. Then narrow with venue/room check-ins + Bluetooth confirmation (the hybrid funnel: same city -> same venue -> both active -> BLE encounter).
3. Treat background detection as best-effort and opportunistic, never promised.
4. Only build hardware (a Haven beacon/wearable) after demand is proven, because a dedicated device is the only thing that truly escapes Apple's background ceiling.

When three models built on different training all converge on the same staircase, that's strong evidence it's the actual shape of the constraint, not one AI being pessimistic. GPT's technical pointers are correct too: Multipeer Connectivity and Nearby Interaction are the right frameworks for the foreground radar version, and both note the app must be foreground for reliable ranging - which is the same wall stated as an API fact.

So your own conclusion - "auto-detect is a future thing, not needed now" - is exactly where all the evidence points. Build the Radar as an explicit event mode when you get there, keep the wearable as the "if this moment is magic enough" bet, and don't let it touch the MVP.

My quick take while it thinks: as a solo founder pre-launch, wrapping your existing React + Convex app with Capacitor almost certainly beats a Swift rewrite (you keep everything you've built and still get widgets, App Clips, Bluetooth, calendar), and one datastore beats a hybrid until search actually hurts. But I asked Fable for the fuller reasoning since you wanted its view - I'll relay it the moment it lands.

# Polygres: An AI-Ready Database Layer

**What it is:** Polygres is a PostgreSQL extension that transforms standard Postgres into "working memory for AI agents." It's not a replacement database but rather an enhancement that unifies three data retrieval capabilities within a single Postgres instance.

**Main features:**

Polygres combines three memory types—structured records (tables), connected relationships (graph traversal), and semantic recall (vector search)—into one hybrid query system. Rather than managing separate vector stores or ETL pipelines, developers can retrieve relevant context through a single database call.

The platform offers:
- **Native HNSW vector search** integrated directly into Postgres
- **pgGraph functionality** for traversing database relationships (e.g., orders → payments → disputes)
- **Unified querying** that applies semantic matching, graph hops, and scalar filters simultaneously

**Search capabilities:**

Polygres emphasizes semantic and hybrid retrieval. The example shows agents querying with natural language ("why did order #8231 fail?") while specifying graph depth and token limits—merging vector similarity, relational filters, and relationship traversal in one operation.

**Who it's for:**

AI engineers and teams building agent systems who need their models to access large datasets efficiently. Rather than stuffing entire databases into token-limited prompts, developers can retrieve precisely relevant context on-demand.

Polygres is maintained by Evokoa and available as either managed cloud instances or open-source SDK deployments.

It's pitched as "working memory for AI agents" / GraphRAG on Postgres.

Now the honest part, in two halves.

**Does that shape fit Haven long-term? Yes, genuinely - your instinct is not wrong.** Haven really is a tabular + graph + vector problem once the vision fills in:

- Relational: filter people by company, city, role.
- Graph: the connection network itself. "Who do I know who knows someone at LinkedIn," shared-interest matching, degrees of separation - those are graph traversals, and a document DB models them awkwardly.
- Vector: semantic search over freeform memories and interest-matching ("find people like this").

We build the client natively in SwiftUI rather than wrapping the web app.

Verdict up front: the strategy layer is sound (single-player value first, one foundation change at a time, scope guardrails), but the doc has one internal contradiction, two real architectural gaps, and a handful of things that will bite at App Store submission if we don't plan them. Ranked by how much they matter:

## 1. The doc contradicts itself on the core loop

The engine is stated as Capture -> Refine -> Recall -> Reach. But Refine (use case C) is described entirely through the swipe queue and voice notes - which the scope section parks as out of MVP. So as written, the MVP ships an engine missing one of its four strokes, and the doc never says what Refine looks like in v1.

## 2. "Feel is the product" but feel is scheduled last

Fix: add a hero-interaction spike to Phase 1 - build one moment (the connect animation, or directory scroll + card open) to full quality bar early. It validates both your SwiftUI ceiling and the taste direction, and everything after inherits the standard.

## 3. The capture moment can't depend on connectivity - but right now it does

Events have terrible network (conference basements, crowded bars). Convex is online-first; its Swift client has no durable offline write queue, so a manual save or connect on bad Wi-Fi just fails - at the exact moment the whole product exists for. This is the biggest quiet UX hole in the plan.

Fix: a small local pending queue - capture writes locally first, syncs when network returns, UI shows "pending" instead of an error. Cheap to build, protects the core promise.

## 4. Snapshot vs live-sync is an unmade architectural decision

The doc says connecting "auto-populates a contact row" - that's copy-at-connect-time. But then contacts go stale, which is the exact problem Haven claims to solve ("how do I reach them *now*"). Copy vs reference changes the schema.

Fix: overlay model. A connection-backed contact stores only *your* layer (notes, your custom fields) plus a reference to their live profile; the app renders the merge. Their card stays current, your memories stay yours. This also cleanly answers a question the doc doesn't ask: what happens when someone deletes their account. (My suggested default: their canonical data goes, your contact collapses to a frozen snapshot you own, like a phone contact. Worth a conscious decision either way.)

## 5. The search promise and the MVP search are two different things

Use case D shows natural-language queries ("who do I know at LinkedIn who lives in SF"). MVP search is attribute filters + keyword matching - typing that sentence into a box will return nothing, and the MVP will feel like it broke its one promise. Also, fuzzy matching is limited: "Catrin" may not find "Katrin."

Fix: design the MVP search UI as filter chips (company, city, role) plus a keyword field over notes, and say so in the doc. The natural-language box is explicitly the semantic fast-follow. Set this expectation now or MVP testing will read as failure when it's actually scope.

## 6. App Store realities are missing from the build order

## 7. Phase 0's definition of done is too loose

"One screen reading live data" doesn't de-risk the real integration. The riskiest seam is Clerk-issued JWTs authenticating Convex calls from Swift on a device.

## 8. Smaller but real

- **Contacts have no photo field.** Your own complaint was "they changed their profile picture, you might miss them" - recognition needs faces. Add photo to contacts (and profile photo flows in via the overlay).
- **All-or-nothing card sharing.** Connecting reveals your entire card - every handle, phone included. Real people share selectively. Fine for the trusted cohort; put "selective sharing" on the roadmap because it'll be an early ask.

- **Name check.** "Haven" is a crowded name on the App Store - verify availability early; you may need a "Haven: ..." subtitle form. Cheap to check now, annoying at submission.

# Haven MVP Design

## What Haven is

Haven is a searchable private memory network for the people you know.

You save people, you connect with them through one central hub, and later you find any of them by any detail you remember.

The phone is the product.
You meet people holding your phone, so Haven is phone-first and the feel of the app matters as much as the features.

## The MVP in one sentence

An iPhone app where you have a profile, you connect with people in one tap, and every person you know becomes searchable by any detail you remember about them.

## Stack decisions (and why)

### Client: native SwiftUI

We build the client natively in SwiftUI rather than wrapping the web app.

Haven is a human and social app where the entire value is how it feels to hold, connect, and browse people.
Gesture physics, spring transitions, haptics, momentum scroll, and keyboard behavior are the product, not polish added later.
A WebView has a ceiling on that feel that native does not, so native is the right tool for what we care most about.

Development cost and speed are explicitly not the deciding factor here.
Long-term quality and the tactile experience win.

### Backend: Convex (kept)

We keep Convex as the backend.

Going native is a client rebuild, not a full-system rewrite.
The Convex data model, functions, and auth logic largely persist.
Convex ships a Swift client and Clerk ships an iOS SDK, so the native app talks to the same backend.

Those mobile SDKs are newer and less battle-tested than their web counterparts.
That is the one real cost of going native, and Phase 0 exists to de-risk it before we build anything real on top.

We change one foundation at a time.
Going native is already one big change, so we do not also swap the database at the same moment.

One caveat that shapes the client design: Convex is online-first and its Swift client has no durable offline write queue.
The capture moment happens at events with bad connectivity, so the client owns a small local pending queue (see The offline rule below).

### Auth: Clerk with custom UI

We use Clerk, with fully custom UI.

Clerk supports headless custom flows where we build every screen ourselves in SwiftUI and call Clerk methods underneath.
On iOS this is the normal path, so we get full control of the sign-in and sign-up feel while Clerk carries the security machinery.

We include Sign in with Apple from day one.
App Store guideline 4.8 requires it once any third-party login (for example Google) is offered, and it is also the lowest-friction option for the App Clip later.

We do not build our own auth system.
The hard parts of auth are invisible and dangerous: password hashing, session token rotation, OAuth, verification, rate limiting, and breach handling.
Getting any of those subtly wrong leaks user data, and Haven lives or dies on trust.

### Repo layout

Monorepo.
The iOS app lives in an `ios/` directory next to the existing `convex/` backend and `src/` web app.
The web app stays alive as the waitlist and marketing surface, not as a product client.

### Datastore note: Convex now, revisit later

Haven's long-term data shape is relational plus graph plus vector.
Attributes are relational, the connection network is a graph, and semantic memory search is vector.

That shape fits a Postgres-family system (for example plain managed Postgres with pgvector, or Polygres) better than a pure document store in the long run.

We do not adopt that now.
The MVP needs none of graph traversal or hybrid retrieval, Polygres specifically is a very young product to bet a foundation on, and we refuse to stack two risky rewrites at once.
When the graph and matching phase becomes real, we evaluate the datastore against actual requirements.
Managed Postgres plus pgvector is the safe pick, Polygres is the ambitious one, and the small three-table model keeps migration cheap if we ever move.

## Design principles

The core loop is Capture, Refine, Recall, Reach.
If those feel great, Haven works.
If they do not, no feature saves it.

In the MVP, each stroke of the loop has a concrete form:
Capture is connecting or manually saving a person.
Refine is opening a contact and editing its memory notes.
Recall is search.
Reach is tapping the preferred contact method.
The swipe review queue is the future upgrade of Refine, not its definition, so the MVP notes editor is a money screen and not an afterthought textbox.

Single-player value comes first.
The directory, manual save, and search are useful even if you are the only Haven user in the world, so we build that before the network layer.

Reduce friction at the moment of input.
Input is the hardest thing to get, so every capture step must be fast enough to not break a live conversation.

The offline rule: capture never fails.
Events have terrible network, so every capture action writes locally first and syncs when connectivity returns.
The UI shows pending state, never an error, at the moment of capture.

Feel is validated early, not last.
Phase 1 includes a hero-interaction spike built to the full quality bar, so we learn our SwiftUI ceiling in week two instead of after four phases of plumbing.

Protect the scope.
The vision is large, and every idea will try to pull us off the core, so the roadmap stays parked until the core is proven.

## Scope: what is in, what is out

In for MVP:

Your own profile and shareable card.
Connect with another Haven user in one tap (mutual, no request and accept dance, because the act of connecting in person is the consent).
Manually save a person who is not on Haven yet, including a photo.
A directory of everyone you know.
Memory notes on every contact, with a first-class editing experience.
Search by structured attribute filters plus keyword matching over notes.
A local pending queue so capture works offline.
Sign in with Apple alongside other login options.
In-app account deletion (required by App Store guideline 5.1.1).

Out for MVP, parked but not forgotten:

App Clip connect-back for non-users.
Semantic natural-language search.
The swipe review queue and voice capture (the upgrade of Refine).
LinkedIn scraping and enrichment.
Calendar smart-matching.
Selective card sharing (per-person control of which fields are revealed).
Rotating connect tokens (anti-replay).
Bluetooth radar and ambient detection.
Any social, matching, or feed layer.
The future idea of the system reading your messages to suggest people.

## Data model (Convex)

Three tables. This is the whole backend for MVP.

### profiles

A Haven user's own card, the canonical source of their data.
Fields: name, photo, socials (IG, X, WhatsApp, Telegram, phone, and any other handles), preferred contact method, and structured attributes (city, company, role).

### contacts

Your directory.
Each row is one person you know, and it uses an overlay model.

A contact always stores your layer: memory notes, your own custom fields, and a photo you attached.
If the person is a connected Haven user, the contact also holds a reference to their live profile, and the app renders the merge of their canonical data plus your layer.
If the person is not on Haven, the contact stores their data directly: display name, structured attributes, social handles, preferred contact, photo.

Reference, not copy, for connection-backed contacts.
Copying at connect time would let contacts go stale, which is the exact problem Haven exists to solve.
With the overlay, their card stays current and your memories stay yours.

Search runs over this table (merged view for connection-backed rows).

### connections

Mutual edges between two Haven users.
When two users connect, one edge is created and a contact row appears in each person's directory referencing the other's profile.

### Deletion semantics

When a user deletes their account, their profile and canonical data are removed.
Contacts in other people's directories that referenced the deleted profile collapse to a frozen snapshot owned by the directory owner, like a phone contact.
Your memory of a person is yours, but the live canonical data belongs to them and leaves with them.

The model is deliberately small so it stays portable if we ever leave Convex.

## Screens (SwiftUI)

Onboarding: Clerk sign-in (Sign in with Apple first), then create your profile (name, photo, socials, preferred contact, city, company, role).

My Card: your profile as a card that you show people. Editable.

Connect: start or accept a connection, and save a non-user manually.

Directory (home): the list of your contacts with search on top. Money screen one.

Contact detail with the notes editor: one person's attributes, socials, a tappable preferred-contact that opens straight into WhatsApp or IG or phone, and your memory notes with a first-class editing experience. Money screen two.

Add contact manually: for people not on Haven (name, photo, socials, notes).

Search: filter chips for structured attributes (company, city, role) plus a keyword field over notes, and results.

## The search contract (MVP)

Be honest about what MVP search is, so testing measures scope and not a broken promise.

MVP search answers: filter by company, city, or role, combined with keywords that appear in your notes.
"Company: LinkedIn, city: SF" works.
Keyword "Spain shirt" works if those words are in the note.

MVP search does not answer natural-language sentences.
Typing "who do I know at LinkedIn who lives in SF" into a box is the semantic fast-follow, not v1.
Fuzzy matching is limited, so a misspelled name may not match.

The search UI is designed as filters plus keywords, so users are never invited to type a sentence that will return nothing.

## The connect flow (MVP version)

For v1 we support the both-have-Haven path only.

Two users connect in person, and both directories update mutually with each other's card.
No separate request and accept step, because connecting in person is the consent.

If the other person is not on Haven, you save them manually.
That manual save is the fallback floor.

Known hole, accepted consciously: a screenshot of a connect code works forever for anyone holding the image.
Fine at trusted-cohort scale.
Rotating tokens are the later fix and live on the roadmap.

The App Clip connect-back for non-users is the very next thing after v1.
It is not blocking, because the first small cohort can all be on Haven for testing.

## Core use cases (start to end)

The core loop is Capture, then Refine, then Recall, then Reach, wrapped by onboarding.

### A. Set up my card (onboarding, once)

I download Haven and sign in.
I build my card: photo, name, my handles, and I mark the one I actually want people to reach me on.
I add where I live, where I work, and my role.
Now I have a card I can show anyone, and I am findable by the people I connect with.

### B. Meet someone and capture them (Capture)

I am at an event and meet someone.
If they have Haven, we connect and their card lands in my directory instantly with all their details, no typing.
If they do not, I add them in a few seconds with a name, a handle, and a quick note.
Either way they are now in my directory, captured without breaking the conversation, even if the venue Wi-Fi is dead.

### C. Add context (Refine)

Later that night I open Haven, go to the person I met, and drop a memory into their notes: "met at Katrin, wore a Spain shirt, works on Amazon's research team, we talked soccer."
Thirty seconds, and the person is richly remembered instead of a blank name I will forget.

The future version of this step is the swipe queue: a stack of today's people, swipe left to skip, swipe right to keep and drop a voice or text memory.
The MVP version is the notes editor, which is why the notes editor has to be excellent.

### D. Find someone by what I remember (Recall)

Weeks later I need that person but I have forgotten their name.
I filter by company LinkedIn and city SF, or I search the keyword "Spain shirt."
Haven pulls them up.
This is the thing other apps cannot do, because they only search by name or a username that might have changed, while Haven searches by everything I know about a person.

The natural-language version of this ("who was the guy in the Spain shirt from Katrin") arrives with semantic search as the first fast-follow.

### E. Reach out (Reach)

I found them, and their card shows the contact method they actually want to be reached on.
I tap it and it opens straight into WhatsApp or IG or their number.
I never had to remember which platform they prefer or dig through five apps, because Haven centralized it.

Everything on the roadmap just makes one of these steps lower-friction or richer.

## Build order

We sequence so something useful exists as early as possible.
The directory, manual save, and search have single-player value, so we build that before the network.

### Phase 0, Foundations

Apple Developer account, Xcode and SwiftUI project in `ios/`, wire in the Convex Swift client and Clerk iOS SDK.

Definition of done, and it is strict: sign in with Clerk on a physical iPhone, call an authenticated Convex query with the Clerk-issued token, and see a live update pushed to the screen.
Reading public data does not count.
The authenticated seam is the riskiest integration in the whole plan, and Phase 0 exists to prove it end to end.

Also in Phase 0: verify App Store name availability for "Haven" (the name is crowded, and a "Haven: ..." subtitle form may be needed).

### Phase 1, Profile plus the hero spike

Onboarding, create and edit profile, My Card.

Plus the hero-interaction spike: one moment (the connect animation, or directory scroll and card open) built to the full quality bar with real springs, haptics, and gesture physics.
This validates our SwiftUI ceiling early and sets the standard everything else inherits.

### Phase 2, Directory, manual save, contact detail

Now you can save and open people, and the app is dogfoodable immediately.
The local pending queue ships here, because capture must never fail offline.
The notes editor ships here and gets money-screen treatment.

### Phase 3, Search

Filter chips plus keyword search over the directory, per the search contract above.

### Phase 4, Connect

Connect two Haven users with an auto mutual connection, turning a private notebook into a network.

### Phase 5, Polish pass

Haptics, transitions, and gesture physics across every screen, extending the hero-spike standard to the whole app.
For Haven this is the product, so it gets its own real phase, not leftover time.

### Phase 6, Distribution

TestFlight to the waitlist cohort first, then App Store submission.
Submission needs the compliance checklist below done.

## App Store compliance checklist

In-app account deletion (guideline 5.1.1), wired to the deletion semantics above.
Sign in with Apple offered alongside any third-party login (guideline 4.8).
Privacy policy URL and App Privacy nutrition labels.
Permission strings for camera (connect scanning) and photo library (contact photos).

## Testing strategy

Convex functions keep the existing vitest TDD flow: write the failing test, implement, run the suite.
The Swift side gets view-model unit tests for logic (search filtering, pending queue, merge rendering of overlay contacts).
UI feel is verified by hand on device, because springs and haptics cannot be asserted in a unit test, but everything with logic in it is test-first.

## Roadmap (fast-follows and later)

In rough order after MVP.

Semantic natural-language search, the AI-directory magic, using Convex vector search over memory notes.

App Clip connect-back, so a non-user can join the connection in the moment with a single Sign in with Apple tap, without an install wall.

The swipe review queue with voice capture, upgrading Refine from the notes editor to a thirty-second nightly ritual.

LinkedIn enrichment, where you paste a profile link and Haven scrapes it into structured, searchable data.

Calendar smart-matching, where the time you connected with someone plus your calendar pre-fills "met at X" for you to confirm or edit.

Selective card sharing, per-person control over which fields a connection reveals, because all-or-nothing sharing will be an early user ask.

Rotating connect tokens, closing the screenshot-replay hole.

Bluetooth radar as an explicit foreground event mode, and only later a wearable beacon if demand proves out.

The social and matching layer, opt-in and machine-only, where shared interests surface abstract matches without exposing the underlying data.

The far-future idea of the system reading your messages to suggest people, noted only so we do not lose it.

## Open questions and risks

The Convex Swift client and Clerk iOS SDK are newer than their web versions.
This is the main technical risk, mitigated by Phase 0's strict definition of done.

WebView was rejected precisely because of gesture feel, so native quality is now on us to deliver, starting with the Phase 1 hero spike rather than waiting for Phase 5.

Real-world validation has a cold-start trap: at actual events, strangers will not have Haven, so most capture falls to manual entry until the App Clip ships.
Judge the MVP on single-player value (do testers return to search their directory), not on network effects it cannot have yet.

The datastore may need to move to a Postgres-family system when the graph and matching phase arrives, and we accept re-evaluating it then rather than now.

## Concerns

These are the unsolved friction problems at the heart of the product.
They are mostly behavioral and psychological, not technical, which is what makes them hard.
None of them are blockers, but they are the things most likely to decide whether Haven actually works.

### 1. Friction to manually add people

Manual entry is slow relative to a live conversation.
It is framed as the fallback floor, but until the App Clip ships it is the default path at real events, because most strangers will not have Haven.
So the piece we treated as an edge case carries most of the early capture load, and if it feels like data entry people will not do it mid-conversation.
The open question is how fast and low-effort we can make manual add, and whether there is a lighter in-the-moment gesture than filling a form.

### 2. Friction to manually add dynamic context

Dynamic context is the memory only a human holds: how you think about someone, why they matter, the detail you would forget.
There is probably no machine shortcut here, because no scrape or API can know what is in your head, so this input is inherently manual.
That means the lever is not technical, it is psychological: how do we trigger the moment, and how do we make putting it in feel frictionless or even rewarding rather than like a chore.
Direction worth exploring: the right timing of the prompt, making the act feel like a small reward, and the lightest possible input (a sentence, a voice note) instead of structured fields.
This is an open design problem, not a solved one.

### 3. Swipe-to-approve context assumes re-engagement that may not happen

The swipe review ritual assumes people open the app later, on the couch, to process the day.
Many will not.
Deferred review depends on re-engagement that we cannot count on, so the whole "nightly ritual" model may be fragile.
The open question is whether context should be captured more in the moment instead of deferred, or whether a well-timed reminder can reliably pull people back, and this is exactly why the swipe queue is a fast-follow to test rather than an MVP assumption.

## Open questions and risks

Before I pour effort into the scaffold, let me get the approach checked.

Approach is sound - compiler-as-ground-truth over doc-guessing is exactly right. Reinforce it: stop fetching more Clerk docs now. The resolved package sources under DerivedData/SourcePackages are the real API surface; read those when you need a signature. Three things sharpen this, none of them block you from starting.

**Collapse the uncertain surface - you don't need the custom sign-in APIs for Phase 0.** All your remaining uncertainty is in `SignIn.create`/`attemptFirstFactor`/`getToken(template:)`. The whole job of `ClerkConvexAuthProvider` is to observe the Clerk session and fetch the "convex" template token *internally* - so your hand-written code is just four calls from the verified spine: `Clerk.configure` -> present `ClerkKitUI`'s prebuilt auth view -> `ConvexClientWithAuth(deploymentUrl:, authProvider: ClerkConvexAuthProvider())` -> subscribe to one authenticated query. Zero hand-written token/sign-in plumbing, which is precisely the part you couldn't pin down. Custom sign-in UI is a Phase 1 concern anyway (the doc puts onboarding/profile there) - using prebuilt to prove the *seam* doesn't violate the custom-UI decision, it just doesn't build the final screen yet. For the query, reuse the existing my-profile query in `profiles.ts` (it already gates on `requireUser`) instead of adding one.

**Walking skeleton, so pipeline pain surfaces before you've built on it.** `brew install xcodegen` -> project.yml with app target + 3 deps -> generate -> get the near-empty app to a green simulator build *first* -> only then add the four wiring calls -> green again. Stop and report that as the Phase 0 finding. "This integration path isn't mature enough yet" is a real, valuable result - not a failure to grind past.

**Be honest about what green proves, in the PR body.** A simulator build proves the code compiles against the real SDKs and the deps resolve. It does NOT prove auth works - nothing executes in a build. That's fine for a foundations PR, but say it plainly: builds green, not yet run; to finish the Phase 0 DoD the user adds the Clerk publishable key + Convex URL, creates the "convex" JWT template in Clerk, and runs on device. The user greenlit Phase 0 *before* you stated the device handoff, so make the PR unambiguous rather than let it surprise them. And keep sight of this: that green build IS your value here - it's what separates a real foundation from plausible-looking guesses - so it's worth pushing through normal pipeline friction to get, just not the indefinite grind.

Net: go. The prebuilt-UI move is the one that most reduces your risk - take it.

9	/// An AuthProvider implementation that bridges Clerk authentication with Convex.
10	///
11	/// This provider uses Clerk's session management and JWT token generation
12	/// to authenticate with a Convex backend. It automatically listens for token
13	/// refresh events and pushes fresh tokens to Convex.
14	///
15	/// ## Usage
16	///
17	/// ```swift
18	/// let client = ConvexClientWithAuth(
19	///   deploymentUrl: "YOUR_CONVEX_DEPLOYMENT_URL",
20	///   authProvider: ClerkConvexAuthProvider()
21	/// )
22	/// ```
23	///
24	/// - Important: Users must first sign in using Clerk.
25	///   This provider then syncs Convex authentication
26	///   automatically; no manual `client.login()` call is required.
27	@MainActor
28	public final class ClerkConvexAuthProvider: AuthProvider {
29	  public typealias T = String
30	
31	  /// Callback to notify Convex of token updates.
32	  private var onIdToken: (@Sendable (String?) -> Void)?
33	
34	  /// Task that listens for token refresh events.
35	  private var tokenRefreshListenerTask: Task<Void, Never>?
36	
37	  /// Task that syncs Clerk session state with Convex.
38	  private var sessionSyncTask: Task<Void, Never>?
39	
40	  /// Weak reference to the Convex client for session sync.
41	  private weak var client: ConvexClientWithAuth<String>?
42	
43	  /// Creates a new ClerkConvexAuthProvider.
44	  public init() {}
45	
46	  /// Binds a Convex client to this auth provider and starts session sync.
47	  ///
48	  /// This automatically performs an initial sync and listens for Clerk session changes,
49	  /// calling `loginFromCache()` or `logout()` on the client as needed.
50	  ///
51	  /// - Important: `Clerk.configure(...)` must be called before binding.
52	  public func bind(client: ConvexClientWithAuth<String>) {
53	    self.client = client
54	    startSessionSync()
55	  }
56	
57	  /// Retrieves a JWT token from the current Clerk session and sets up token refresh listening.
58	  ///
59	  /// - Parameter onIdToken: Callback to invoke with fresh tokens. Store this and call it
60	  ///   whenever tokens are refreshed.
61	  /// - Returns: A JWT token string for Convex authentication.
62	  /// - Throws: `ClerkConvexAuthError.clerkNotLoaded` if Clerk hasn't finished loading.
63	  /// - Throws: `ClerkConvexAuthError.noActiveSession` if no user is signed in.
64	  /// - Throws: `ClerkConvexAuthError.tokenRetrievalFailed` if token retrieval fails.
65	  public func login(onIdToken: @Sendable @escaping (String?) -> Void) async throws -> String {
66	    try await authenticate(onIdToken: onIdToken)
67	  }
68	
69	  /// Retrieves a JWT token from the current Clerk session using cached credentials.
70	  ///
71	  /// This method attempts to return a cached token if available and not expired,
72	  /// avoiding unnecessary network requests. It also sets up token refresh listening.
73	  ///
74	  /// - Parameter onIdToken: Callback to invoke with fresh tokens. Store this and call it
75	  ///   whenever tokens are refreshed.
76	  /// - Returns: A JWT token string for Convex authentication.
77	  /// - Throws: `ClerkConvexAuthError.clerkNotLoaded` if Clerk hasn't finished loading.
78	  /// - Throws: `ClerkConvexAuthError.noActiveSession` if no user is signed in.
79	  /// - Throws: `ClerkConvexAuthError.tokenRetrievalFailed` if token retrieval fails.
80	  public func loginFromCache(onIdToken: @Sendable @escaping (String?) -> Void) async throws -> String {
81	    try await authenticate(onIdToken: onIdToken)
82	  }
83	
84	  /// Signs out of the current Clerk session.
85	  ///
86	  /// This will end the active Clerk session, notify Convex of the logout,
87	  /// and stop listening for token refresh events.
88	  public func logout() async throws {
89	    tokenRefreshListenerTask?.cancel()
90	    tokenRefreshListenerTask = nil
91	    onIdToken = nil
92	    try await Clerk.shared.auth.signOut()
93	  }
94	
95	  /// Extracts the JWT ID token from the authentication result.
96	  ///
97	  /// Since our `T` type is already a `String` (the JWT token), this
98	  /// method simply returns the input unchanged.
99	  ///
100	  /// - Parameter authResult: The JWT token string.
101	  /// - Returns: The same JWT token string.
102	  public nonisolated func extractIdToken(from authResult: String) -> String {
103	    authResult
104	  }
105	
106	  // MARK: - Private
107	
108	  /// Common implementation for login and loginFromCache.
109	  ///
110	  /// Stores the callback, sets up the token refresh listener, and returns the current token.
111	  private func authenticate(onIdToken: @Sendable @escaping (String?) -> Void) async throws -> String {
112	    self.onIdToken = onIdToken
113	    let token = try await fetchToken()
114	    setupTokenRefreshListener()
115	    return token
116	  }
117	
118	  /// Fetches a JWT token from the active Clerk session.
119	  ///
120	  /// - Returns: A JWT token string for Convex authentication.
121	  /// - Throws: `ClerkConvexAuthError.clerkNotLoaded` if Clerk hasn't finished loading.
122	  /// - Throws: `ClerkConvexAuthError.noActiveSession` if no user is signed in.
123	  /// - Throws: `ClerkConvexAuthError.tokenRetrievalFailed` if the token is nil.
124	  private func fetchToken() async throws -> String {
125	    guard Clerk.shared.isLoaded else {
126	      throw ClerkConvexAuthError.clerkNotLoaded
127	    }
128	
129	    guard let session = Clerk.shared.session, session.status == .active else {
130	      throw ClerkConvexAuthError.noActiveSession
131	    }
132	
133	    guard let token = try await session.getToken() else {
134	      throw ClerkConvexAuthError.tokenRetrievalFailed("Token returned nil")
135	    }
136	
137	    return token
138	  }
139	
140	  /// Sets up a listener for Clerk auth events to handle token refresh.
141	  ///
142	  /// Note: Session changes are handled by the session sync started via `bind(client:)`,
143	  /// which triggers `loginFromCache()` or `logout()` on the Convex client. This listener
144	  /// only handles ongoing token refreshes while authenticated.
145	  private func setupTokenRefreshListener() {
146	    tokenRefreshListenerTask?.cancel()
147	
148	    tokenRefreshListenerTask = Task { [weak self] in
149	      guard let self else { return }
150	
151	      for await event in Clerk.shared.auth.events {
152	        guard !Task.isCancelled else { break }
153	
154	        switch event {
155	        case .tokenRefreshed(let token):
156	          onIdToken?(token)
157	        default:
158	          break
159	        }
160	      }
161	    }
162	  }
163	
164	  /// Starts syncing Clerk session state with the bound Convex client.
165	  private func startSessionSync() {
166	    sessionSyncTask?.cancel()
167	
168	    sessionSyncTask = Task { @MainActor [weak self] in
169	      guard let self else { return }
170	
171	      await syncSession(newSession: Clerk.shared.session)
172	
173	      for await event in Clerk.shared.auth.events {
174	        guard !Task.isCancelled else { break }
175	
176	        switch event {
177	        case .sessionChanged(let oldSession, let newSession):
178	          await syncSession(oldSession: oldSession, newSession: newSession)
179	        default:
180	          break
181	        }
182	      }
183	    }
184	  }
185	
186	  /// Syncs a Clerk session transition with the Convex client.
187	  ///
188	  /// Convex login only runs when a session transitions from non-active to active.
189	  /// Convex logout runs when a session transitions from any value to nil.
190	  private func syncSession(oldSession: Session? = nil, newSession: Session?) async {
191	    guard let client else { return }
192	
193	    if shouldLogin(oldSession: oldSession, newSession: newSession) {
194	      _ = await client.loginFromCache()
195	    } else if shouldLogout(oldSession: oldSession, newSession: newSession) {
196	      await client.logout()
197	    }
198	  }
199	
200	  /// Returns true when we should authenticate Convex from cached Clerk credentials.
201	  private func shouldLogin(oldSession: Session?, newSession: Session?) -> Bool {
202	    newSession?.status == .active &&
203	    (oldSession?.status != .active || oldSession?.id != newSession?.id)
204	  }
205	
206	  /// Returns true when we should clear Convex auth due to session removal.
207	  private func shouldLogout(oldSession: Session?, newSession: Session?) -> Bool {
208	    oldSession?.id != nil && newSession == nil
209	  }
210	}

40	  ///   - name: A value in "module:query_name"  format that will be used when calling the backend
41	  ///   - args: An optional ``Dictionary`` of arguments to be sent to the backend query function
42	  ///   - output: The type of data that will be returned in the Publisher, as a convenience to callers
43	  ///             where the type can't be easily inferred.
44	  public func subscribe<T: Decodable>(
45	    to name: String, with args: [String: ConvexEncodable?]? = nil, yielding output: T.Type? = nil
46	  ) -> AnyPublisher<T, ClientError> {
47	    // There are two steps to producing the final Publisher in this method.
48	    // 1. Subscribe to the data from Convex and publish the subscription handle
49	    // 2. Feed the subscription handle into the Convex data Publisher so it can cancel the upstream
50	    //    subscription when downstream subscribers are done consuming data
51	
52	    // This Publisher will ultimately publish the data received from Convex.
53	    let convexPublisher = PassthroughSubject<T, ClientError>()
54	    let adapter = SubscriptionAdapter<T>(publisher: convexPublisher)
55	
56	    // This Publisher is responsible for initializing the Convex subscription and returning a handle
57	    // to the upstream (Convex) subscription.
58	    let initializationPublisher = Future<SubscriptionHandle, ClientError> {
59	      result in
60	      Task {
61	        do {
62	          let subscriptionHandle = try await self.ffiClient.subscribe(
63	            name: name,
64	            args: args?.mapValues({ v in
65	              try v?.convexEncode() ?? "null"
66	            }) ?? [:], subscriber: adapter)
67	          result(.success(subscriptionHandle))
68	        } catch {
69	          result(.failure(ClientError.InternalError(msg: error.localizedDescription)))
70	        }
71	      }
72	    }
73	
74	    // The final Publisher takes the handle from the initial Convex subscription and supplies it to
75	    // the data publisher so it can cancel the upstream subscription when consumers are no longer
76	    // listening for data.
77	    return initializationPublisher.flatMap({ subscriptionHandle in
78	      convexPublisher.handleEvents(receiveCancel: {
79	        subscriptionHandle.cancel()
80	      })
81	    })
82	    .eraseToAnyPublisher()
83	  }

input.content:
# Haven iOS (Phase 0 foundations)

This is the native SwiftUI client scaffold for Haven.
Its only job in Phase 0 is to prove the riskiest seam in the whole native plan: Clerk sign-in on iOS authenticating a real Convex query.

See `../mvp-design.md` for the full plan. Phase 0's strict definition of done is: sign in with Clerk on a physical iPhone, call an authenticated Convex query, and see a live result.

## Status

The scaffold is written against the pinned SDK versions and mirrors the `clerk-convex-swift` package's own example app, so the integration pattern is verified.
What a green build proves and does not prove:

- A green simulator build proves the code compiles against the real SDKs and the Swift packages resolve and link.
- It does NOT prove authentication works, because nothing executes during a build.

Finishing the Phase 0 DoD is a human step: add the two config values, create the Clerk JWT template, and run on a device (below).

## Prerequisites

- Xcode 26.x with an installed iOS simulator runtime (open Xcode once, or run `xcodebuild -downloadPlatform iOS`).
- XcodeGen: `brew install xcodegen`.

## Generate and open

The `.xcodeproj` is generated from `project.yml` and is git-ignored.

```sh
cd ios
xcodegen generate
open Haven.xcodeproj
```

## Configure (required before running)

1. Edit `Haven/Config.swift`:
   - `clerkPublishableKey` from the Clerk dashboard (API keys).
   - `convexDeploymentUrl`, e.g. `https://brilliant-puma-925.convex.cloud` (the dev deployment).
   Both values are public and safe to ship in the app binary.
2. In the Clerk dashboard, create a JWT template named `convex` (the Convex integration template).
3. On the Convex deployment, set `CLERK_JWT_ISSUER_DOMAIN` to the Clerk Frontend API URL: `npx convex env set CLERK_JWT_ISSUER_DOMAIN <domain>`.
   This is already read by `convex/auth.config.ts`, which pins `applicationID: "convex"`.

## Run

Build to a simulator or a device.
Signed out, you get Clerk's prebuilt `AuthView`.
Signed in, the app calls `profiles:getMyProfile` (auth-gated by `requireUser`) and shows the result.
Seeing "Signed in" (with or without a profile row) means the authenticated Convex call succeeded end to end.

## Compile-check from the command line

```sh
xcodegen generate
xcodebuild build -project Haven.xcodeproj -scheme Haven \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 16' \
  CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO
```

## Architecture notes

- Dependencies (SPM, pinned in `project.yml`): `ConvexMobile` (convex-swift), `ClerkKit` + `ClerkKitUI` (clerk-ios), `ClerkConvex` (clerk-convex-swift).
- `convex` is a single app-lifetime `ConvexClientWithAuth` using `ClerkConvexAuthProvider()`. The provider watches the Clerk session and fetches the `convex` template token itself; there is no manual login call.
- Sign-in uses Clerk's prebuilt `AuthView` for now. The custom sign-in UI is Phase 1 work; Phase 0 only needs to prove the seam.
- `AuthModel` mirrors the client's `authState`; `ProfileModel` subscribes to the auth-gated query.

description: Haven's product/tech direction decided 2026-07-23 -- native SwiftUI iOS client, mvp-design.md is the source of truth, Phase 0 auth seam shipped
