Decided 2026-07-23: Haven's first real client is a **native SwiftUI iOS app**, not a PWA or Capacitor wrap.
Reason the user gave: this is a human/social app where the tactile feel (gestures, springs, haptics) IS the product, and development cost/speed is explicitly not a constraint. So the WebView ceiling is unacceptable and native is worth the rebuild.

Backend stays **Convex + Clerk** (Clerk with custom UI later; Clerk supports headless flows so no need to build own auth). Datastore stays Convex for the MVP; move to a Postgres-family system (plain Postgres+pgvector is the safe pick, Polygres the ambitious one) only if the graph/matching/search phase actually hurts later. Do not stack that migration on top of the native rebuild.

**`mvp-design.md` (repo root) is the single source of truth** for the MVP: core loop Capture->Refine->Recall->Reach, three-table Convex model (profiles/contacts/connections with an overlay model), phased build (Phase 0 foundations through Phase 6 distribution), plus a Concerns section on input-friction (the hardest, mostly behavioral, problem). Shipped as PR #49 (branch docs/mvp-design).

content.text:
For just running it on the simulator: yes. The two values in `Config.swift` are all the app needs, and the simulator needs no Apple Developer signing (that's only for a physical device). It'll build and launch.

But there's an important distinction between "it runs" and "sign-in actually succeeds," because I verified how the token flow works: the iOS SDK fetches your Clerk session token and hands it to Convex, and Convex only accepts it if the **backend** is configured to trust your Clerk instance. That config lives on the Convex deployment, not in `Config.swift`:

- `CLERK_JWT_ISSUER_DOMAIN` must be set on the Convex deployment (it's what `convex/auth.config.ts` reads).
- Your Clerk instance must be set up for Convex so the token it mints is accepted.

Here's the good news that probably saves you all of that: **your web app already signs into the same Convex dev deployment.** That means the backend is very likely already wired for your dev Clerk instance. So the move is:

1. Use the **same** Clerk publishable key and Convex URL your web app already uses - grab them from your `.env.local` (`VITE_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` and the Convex URL, which is the `brilliant-puma-925` dev deployment). Don't invent new ones.
2. Put those two into `Config.swift`.
3. Run on iPhone 17.

If those are the values that already work for web, sign-in on iOS should just work, and you'll land on "Authenticated" with your profile (or the "no profile row yet" line).

One honest caveat: the iOS provider fetches Clerk's *default* session token, whereas web clients sometimes fetch a named "convex" template token. If those carry different audience claims, you could sign in via Clerk but hit the red **"Convex call failed"** - that's the probe correctly telling you the token was rejected, not a crash. If you see that, tell me and I'll align the Clerk/Convex token config; it's a small backend setting, not an app problem.

So: to *run* it - yes, the keys are all you need. To *prove sign-in end-to-end* - use your existing web dev values, and the red-error case (if it happens) is a quick backend fix I'll handle.

Found it and fixed it. Here's the short version of the root cause, proven from source (not a guess):

- Your **web** app authenticates through `ConvexProviderWithClerk`, which fetches the token with `getToken({ template: "convex" })` - so its token's audience is `"convex"`, matching `applicationID: "convex"` in `convex/auth.config.ts`.
- The **iOS** glue package calls `session.getToken()` with no template, sending Clerk's default token with a different audience. Convex refuses it, retries auth in a loop, and never runs the query - which is exactly the endless spinner you saw.

The fix: I added a Haven-owned auth provider that mints the same `"convex"`-template token as your web app. It's a faithful copy of the glue's logic with that one change (plus I made the ~60-second token refresh re-fetch the templated token, so it won't break after the first minute). No backend or web changes, so your working web app is untouched. It builds green.

Now I have the actual root cause from the logs, and it's not the app logic at all - it's my build:

```
Keychain operation failed with OSStatus -34018: A required entitlement isn't present.
... 401 signed_out "You are signed out"
```

`-34018` means the app has no keychain entitlement, so Clerk can't save its device token to the keychain, and every request comes back as `401 signed_out`. This is because I built from the command line with **code signing turned off** - so the app has no entitlements at all. Clerk iOS requires Keychain access. When *you* Run from Xcode, it signs the app and this wouldn't happen. So "from your version" it fails specifically because my CLI build was unsigned - it's a build/signing artifact, not a bug in the auth code. Good news, really.

Two things: the project should declare the Keychain Sharing capability (Clerk needs it, and real devices will too), and then we merge to main so you test from a properly-signed Xcode build - exactly what you suggested. Let me add the entitlement, verify the keychain error is gone with a signed build, then consolidate to main.

gh pr create --base main --head fix/ios-clerk-auth --title "fix(ios): make Clerk sign-in authenticate Convex (keychain entitlement + convex token template)" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## TLDR

The Phase 0 iOS app could sign in with Clerk but the screen hung forever, and in some builds sign-in failed outright with "You are signed out." Two separate root causes, both fixed here. After this, signing in on iOS actually reaches an authenticated Convex query, which is the whole point of Phase 0.

## Two fixes

**1. Convex token audience (the hang).**
The web app authenticates via `ConvexProviderWithClerk`, which fetches the token with `getToken({ template: "convex" })` - audience `"convex"`, matching `applicationID: "convex"` in `convex/auth.config.ts`. The stock `ClerkConvexAuthProvider` calls `session.getToken()` with no template, so its token had a different audience, Convex rejected it, and the auth-gated query hung. Replace it with a Haven-owned provider that mints the `"convex"` template token (the refresh path re-fetches the templated token too, since Clerk tokens expire ~60s).

**2. Keychain entitlement (the "signed out" error).**
Clerk iOS stores its device token in the keychain. Without a `keychain-access-groups` entitlement the app fails with `OSStatus -34018` and every sign-in returns `401 signed_out`. Add a Keychain Sharing entitlement and wire `CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS` in `project.yml`.

## Verification

- Builds green on the iOS 26.5 simulator.
- With a signed build, the launch-time keychain errors (`-34018`) are gone from the logs, clearing the "You are signed out" wall.
- No backend or web changes; the web app is untouched.

Follow-up to the merged Phase 0 scaffold (#50). Config keys already landed on main via #51.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

7	
8	A prototype is **throwaway code that answers a question**. The question decides the shape.

10	## Pick a branch
11	
12	Identify which question is being answered — from the user's prompt, the surrounding code, or by asking if the user is around:
13	
14	- **"Does this logic / state model feel right?"** → [LOGIC.md](LOGIC.md). Build a tiny interactive terminal app that pushes the state machine through cases that are hard to reason about on paper.

16	
17	The two branches produce very different artifacts — getting this wrong wastes the whole prototype. If the question is genuinely ambiguous and the user isn't reachable, default to whichever branch better matches the surrounding code (a backend module → logic; a page or component → UI) and state the assumption at the top of the prototype.
18	
19	## Rules that apply to both
20	
21	1. **Throwaway from day one, and clearly marked as such.** Locate the prototype code close to where it will actually be used (next to the module or page it's prototyping for) so context is obvious — but name it so a casual reader can see it's a prototype, not production. For throwaway UI routes, obey whatever routing convention the project already uses; don't invent a new top-level structure.
22	2. **One command to run.** Whatever the project's existing task runner supports — `pnpm <name>`, `python <path>`, `bun <path>`, etc. The user must be able to start it without thinking.
23	3. **No persistence by default.** State lives in memory. Persistence is the thing the prototype is _checking_, not something it should depend on. If the question explicitly involves a database, hit a scratch DB or a local file with a clear "PROTOTYPE — wipe me" name.
24	4. **Skip the polish.** No tests, no error handling beyond what makes the prototype _runnable_, no abstractions. The point is to learn something fast.
25	5. **Surface the state.** After every action (logic) or on every variant switch (UI), print or render the full relevant state so the user can see what changed.
26	6. **Capture it when done.** Fold any validated decision into the real code, then capture the prototype itself as a **primary source**: commit it to a throwaway branch, out of main, and leave a context pointer to that branch on the implementation issue. 48	Draft each variant. Hold each one to:
49	
50	- The page's purpose and the data it has access to.
51	- The project's component library / styling system (TailwindCSS, shadcn, MUI, plain CSS, whatever).
52	- A clear exported component name, e.g. `VariantA`, `VariantB`, `VariantC`.
53	
54	Variants must be **structurally different** — different layout, different information hierarchy, different primary affordance, not just different colours. Three slightly-tweaked card grids isn't a UI prototype, it's wallpaper. If two drafts come out too similar, redo one with explicit "do not use a card grid" guidance.
55	
56	### 3. Wire them together
57	
58	Create a single switcher component on the route:
59	
60	```tsx
61	// pseudo-code — adapt to the project's framework
62	const variant = searchParams.get('variant') ?? 'A';
63	return (
64	  <>
65	    {variant === 'A' && <VariantA {...data} />}
66	    {variant === 'B' && <VariantB {...data} />}
67	    {variant === 'C' && <VariantC {...data} />}
68	    <PrototypeSwitcher variants={['A','B','C']} current={variant} />
69	  </>
70	);
71	```
72	
73	For sub-shape A (existing page): keep all the existing data fetching above the switcher; only the rendered subtree changes per variant.
74	
75	For sub-shape B (new page): the throwaway route under `/prototype/<name>` mounts the same switcher.
76	
77	### 4. Build the floating switcher
78	
79	A small fixed-position bar at the bottom-centre of the screen with three pieces:
80	
81	- **Left arrow** — cycles to the previous variant (wraps around).
82	- **Variant label** — shows the current variant key and, if the variant exports a name, that name too. e.g. `B — Sidebar layout`.
83	- **Right arrow** — cycles forward (wraps around).
84	
85	Behaviour:
86	
87	- Clicking an arrow updates the URL search param (use the framework's router — `router.replace` on Next, `navigate` on React Router, etc) so the variant is shareable and reload-stable.
88	- Keyboard: `←` and `→` arrow keys also cycle. Don't intercept arrow keys when an `<input>`, `<textarea>`, or `[contenteditable]` is focused.
89	- Visually distinct from the page (e.g. high-contrast pill, subtle shadow) so it's obviously not part of the design being evaluated.
90	- Hidden in production builds — gate on `process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'` or an equivalent check, so a stray prototype merge can't ship the bar to users.
91	
92	Put the switcher in a single shared component so both sub-shapes can reuse it. Locate it wherever shared UI lives in the project.
93	
94	### 5. Hand it over
95	
96	Surface the URL (and the `?variant=` keys). The user will flip through whenever they get to it. The interesting feedback is usually **"I want the header from B with the sidebar from C"** — that's the actual design they want.
97	
98	### 6. Capture the answer and clean up
99	
100	Once a variant has won, capture the answer — which variant and why — then capture the prototype the way the [SKILL](SKILL.md) describes. Fold the winner into the real code and move the rest onto the throwaway branch, not into main:
101	
102	- **Sub-shape A** — fold the winner into the existing page; drop the losing variants and the switcher from main.
103	- **Sub-shape B** — promote the winning variant to a real route; drop the throwaway route and the switcher from main.
104	
105	The full set of variants is the primary source, so it lands on the throwaway branch, not the bin — variant components and the switcher left in the main branch rot fast and confuse the next reader.
106	
107	## Anti-patterns
108	
109	- **Variants that differ only in colour or copy.** That's a tweak, not a prototype. Real variants disagree about structure.
110	- **Sharing too much code between variants.** A shared `<Header>` is fine; a shared `<Layout>` defeats the point. Each variant should be free to throw out the layout.
111	- **Wiring variants to real mutations.** Read-only prototypes are fine. If a variant needs to mutate, point it at a stub — the question is "what should this look like", not "does the backend work".
112	- **Promoting the prototype directly to production.** The variant code was written under prototype constraints (no tests, minimal error handling). Rewrite it properly when you fold it in.
113

1	# Logic Prototype
2	
3	A tiny interactive terminal app that lets the user drive a state model by hand. Use this when the question is about **business logic, state transitions, or data shape** — the kind of thing that looks reasonable on paper but only feels wrong once you push it through real cases.
4	
5	## When this is the right shape
6	
7	- "I'm not sure if this state machine handles the edge case where X then Y."
8	- "Does this data model actually let me represent the case where..."
9	- "I want to feel out what the API should look like before writing it."
10	- Anything where the user wants to **press buttons and watch state change**.
11	
12	If the question is "what should this look like" — wrong branch. Use [UI.md](UI.md).
13	
14	## Process
15	
16	### 1. State the question
17	
18	Before writing code, write down what state model and what question you're prototyping. One paragraph, in the prototype's README or a comment at the top of the file. A logic prototype that answers the wrong question is pure waste — make the question explicit so it can be checked later, whether the user is watching now or returning to it AFK.
19	
20	### 2. Pick the language
21	
22	Use whatever the host project uses. If the project has no obvious runtime (e.g. a docs repo), ask.
23	
24	Match the project's existing conventions for tooling — don't add a new package manager or runtime just for the prototype.
25	
26	### 3. Isolate the logic in a portable module
27	
28	Put the actual logic — the bit that's answering the question — behind a small, pure interface that could be lifted out and dropped into the real codebase later. The TUI around it is throwaway; the logic module shouldn't be.
29	
30	The right shape depends on the question:
31	
32	- **A pure reducer** — `(state, action) => state`. Good when actions are discrete events and state is a single value.
33	- **A state machine** — explicit states and transitions. Good when "which actions are even legal right now" is part of the question.
34	- **A small set of pure functions** over a plain data type. Good when there's no implicit current state — just transformations.
35	- **A class or module with a clear method surface** when the logic genuinely owns ongoing internal state.
36	
37	Pick whichever shape best fits the question being asked, *not* whichever is easiest to wire to a TUI. Keep it pure: no I/O, no terminal code, no `console.log` for control flow. The TUI imports it and calls into it; nothing flows the other direction.
38	
39	This is what makes the prototype useful past its own lifetime: when the question's been answered, the validated reducer / machine / function set can be lifted into the real module on its own.
40	
41	### 4. Build the smallest TUI that exposes the state
42	
43	Build it as a **lightweight TUI** — on every tick, clear the screen (`console.clear()` / `print("\033[2J\033[H")` / equivalent) and re-render the whole frame. The user should always see one stable view, not an ever-growing scrollback.
44	
45	Each frame has two parts, in this order:
46	
47	1. **Current state**, pretty-printed and diff-friendly (one field per line, or formatted JSON). Use **bold** for field names or section headers and **dim** for less important context (timestamps, IDs, derived values). Native ANSI escape codes are fine — `\x1b[1m` bold, `\x1b[2m` dim, `\x1b[0m` reset. No need to pull in a styling library unless one is already in the project.
48	2. **Keyboard shortcuts**, listed at the bottom: `[a] add user  [d] delete user  [t] tick clock  [q] quit`. Bold the key, dim the description, or vice-versa — whatever reads cleanly.
49	
50	Behaviour:
51	
52	1. **Initialise state** — a single in-memory object/struct. Render the first frame on start.
53	2. **Read one keystroke (or one line)** at a time, dispatch to a handler that mutates state.
54	3. **Re-render** the full frame after every action — don't append, replace.
55	4. **Loop until quit.**
56	
57	The whole frame should fit on one screen.
58	
59	### 5. Make it runnable in one command
60	
61	Add a script to the project's existing task runner (`package.json` scripts, `Makefile`, `justfile`, `pyproject.toml`). The user should run `pnpm run <prototype-name>` or equivalent — never need to remember a path.
62	
63	If the host project has no task runner, just put the command at the top of the prototype's README.
64	
65	### 6. Hand it over
66	
67	Give the user the run command. They'll drive it themselves; the interesting moments are when they say "wait, that shouldn't be possible" or "huh, I assumed X would be different" — those are the bugs in the _idea_, which is the whole point. If they want new actions added, add them. Prototypes evolve.
68	
69	### 7. Capture the answer and the prototype
70	
71	Once the prototype has answered its question, capture the answer, then capture the prototype the way the [SKILL](SKILL.md) describes. The logic-specific mapping: the validated reducer / machine / function set lifts into the real module (the decision, absorbed); the TUI shell rides along to the throwaway branch that keeps the prototype as a primary source.
72	
73	## Anti-patterns
74	
75	- **Don't add tests.** A prototype that needs tests is no longer a prototype.
76	- **Don't wire it to the real database.** Use an in-memory store unless the question is specifically about persistence.
77	- **Don't generalise.** No "what if we wanted to support X later." The prototype answers one question.
78	- **Don't blur the logic and the TUI together.** If the reducer / state machine references `console.log`, prompts, or terminal escape codes, it's no longer portable. Keep the TUI as a thin shell over a pure module.
79	- **Don't ship the TUI shell into production.** The shell is optimised for being driven by hand from a terminal. The logic module behind it is the bit worth keeping.
80

Read all three files (SKILL.md, LOGIC.md, UI.md). Here's what it actually is and whether it fits us.

## What `/prototype` is

It's a tool for answering **one specific design question** with throwaway code - not a planning tool. The question decides the shape, and there are two branches:

- **LOGIC** - a tiny interactive terminal app where you press keys and watch a state model change. For "does this state machine / data shape actually handle the case where X then Y?" - the kind of thing that reads fine on paper but feels wrong once you push real cases through it.
- **UI** - several radically different visual variations of a screen on one web route, switchable with `?variant=` and a floating bar, so you flip between them and pick.

Both are explicitly throwaway, no tests, no persistence, one command to run.

## Does it fit "re-prototype our plan"?

Honestly, no - not as a whole-plan exercise, and I'd push back on using it that way. Two reasons:

1. **It answers questions, not plans.** Our plan (`mvp-design.md`) is already specified - screens, data model, phases. There's no open *question* the size of "the plan" for a prototype to resolve. Pointing it at the whole plan would just produce throwaway code that re-states decisions we've already made.
2. **The UI branch doesn't fit our stack at all.** It's built for web - `?variant=` URLs, Next/React Router, `process.env.NODE_ENV`. Our client is native SwiftUI. UI exploration for us happens in Xcode with SwiftUI previews and build variants, not this skill. So half the skill is a non-starter for Haven.

## Where it *would* genuinely earn its keep - one spot

There's exactly one place in the plan I'd actually prototype, and it's a perfect fit for the **LOGIC** branch: the **contacts overlay + connection + deletion data model.**

That's the part most likely to be subtly wrong on paper:
- A contact is either a reference to a live Haven profile (merged with your private layer) or a standalone manual entry - does that overlay actually represent every case cleanly?
- What happens on connect (both sides populate), and on account deletion (contact collapses to a frozen snapshot you own)?
- Does search behave right over the merged view?

A 60-line TUI over the pure merge/connect/delete logic would let you press "connect," "edit note," "delete account," "search" and watch the state - and catch a modeling mistake before it's baked into Convex schema *and* SwiftUI screens (expensive to unwind in two places).

But timing matters: that model doesn't become real until **Phase 2 (Directory/contacts)**. The next phase, **Phase 1 (Profile)**, is just your own editable card - simple, no tricky state, nothing to prototype.

## My recommendation

- **Don't re-prototype the plan.** It's solid; move forward.
- **Go straight into Phase 1 (Profile).** No prototype needed.
- **Hold one LOGIC prototype of the overlay/connection/deletion model for right before Phase 2** - that's the single high-value use of this skill for us.

So: want me to start Phase 1 (the profile screen + editable card, wired to the existing Convex `profiles` functions), or would you rather de-risk the data model first with that logic prototype? I'd lean Phase 1 - keep the momentum, prototype the model when we get to contacts.

One housekeeping note: now that #52 is the fix, I can clean up the leftover `.worktrees/feat-ios-foundations` worktree and branch so there's one copy. Want me to do that as part of moving on?
wait so when should i use it?

Simple rule: **use it when you have one specific design question you honestly can't answer by thinking about it - and getting it wrong would be expensive to rip out.** The prototype is fast, disposable code whose only job is to let you *feel* the answer before you commit real work.

The tell is when you catch yourself saying:
- "I'm not sure this state model actually handles the case where X then Y..."
- "I think this data shape works, but let me see it move..."
- "I want to see a few options for this screen before I commit."

That's the moment. Two flavors, depending on the question:

- **"Does this logic/data hold up?"** -> the LOGIC branch. A tiny terminal app where you press keys and watch the state change, hunting for the moment you go "wait, that shouldn't be possible." Best for state machines, data models, API shapes.
- **"What should this look like?"** -> the UI branch. Three structurally different versions of a screen side by side so you stop arguing with vague mockups in your head. (Web only - doesn't fit our SwiftUI app.)

**Don't reach for it when:**
- The answer's already clear or decided. Don't prototype what you already know - just build it.
- It's a whole feature or plan, not a single question. Too big; prototypes answer one thing.
- The real question is "does the backend actually work" - that's a spike or a test, not a design prototype. Prototypes are read-only and about *design feel*, not correctness.
- The decision is cheap to reverse. If building the real thing and changing your mind later is easy, skip the extra step.

The gut check: **prototype when guessing wrong is costly and hard to undo; just build when it's cheap and reversible.**

For Haven, concretely:
- **Worth prototyping (LOGIC):** the contacts overlay + connection + deletion model. Genuinely uncertain, and wrong here means unwinding it in *both* the Convex schema and the SwiftUI screens - expensive. Classic prototype candidate.
- **Not worth it:** the Profile screen. It's decided and simple - prototyping it would just be busywork. Build it.
- **Would want it but wrong tool:** "what should the directory look like." That's a real UI question, but since we're native, you'd explore it with SwiftUI previews in Xcode, not this skill.

So the honest short version: you'll use it maybe once or twice across the whole MVP, at the specific moments you're unsure about a state model or a visual direction - not as a routine step. Most of the time you just build.

# Haven

Haven helps you remember the people you meet.

It is a private, searchable memory of everyone you know.
You save a person, jot down whatever you want to remember about them, and later find them by any detail, not just their name.

(The repo is named "euno", the project's original codename. The product is Haven.)

## Why it exists

Meeting people is easy.
Remembering them is hard.

You meet someone great at an event, connect on some app, and months later you cannot recall their name, where they worked, or how to reach them.
Every platform only lets you search by name or a username that might have changed.
Haven lets you search by everything you actually remember: "who do I know at LinkedIn who lives in SF", or "the person in the Spain shirt from that party".

## What you can do

- Save people you meet, with whatever you want to remember about them.
- Connect with another Haven user in one tap, so their details fill in automatically.
- Search your people by any detail: where they work, where you met, what you talked about.
- Reach them on whatever app they actually use, instead of hunting through five different apps.

The loop is simple: capture a person when you meet them, add a note or two later, then find and reach them whenever you need to.

## Where it is at

Haven is early.
The phone comes first, because that is where you meet people and hold your phone.

- The iPhone app (SwiftUI) is just getting started. The foundation, signing in and talking to the backend, works.
- The backend runs on Convex, with Clerk for sign-in.
- There is a web page for the waitlist.

## Learn more

- `mvp-design.md` is the plan: what we are building first, and why.
- `todo.md` is the running tracker: what is done and what is next.

input.old_string: **Phase 0 shipped** as PR #50 (branch feat/ios-foundations, worktree .worktrees/feat-ios-foundations): an `ios/` XcodeGen project that wires the Convex Swift client + Clerk iOS SDK and probes the auth seam via the existing `profiles:getMyProfile`. Verified with a real green build on the iOS 26.5 simulator; Fable-reviewed. The strict DoD (sign in on a physical iPhone and see the authenticated Convex call succeed) is the user's remaining step -- needs their Clerk publishable key, the "convex" JWT template, and a device.
input.new_string:
**Phase 0 DONE and verified** (merged to main via PRs #50 + #52; config keys #51): an `ios/` XcodeGen project wiring the Convex Swift client + Clerk iOS SDK, probing the auth seam via `profiles:getMyProfile`. Sign-in -> authenticated Convex query is confirmed working on a signed iOS 26.5 simulator build (saw "Authenticated, no profile row yet").

Two non-obvious iOS gotchas fixed along the way (code lives in ios/Haven/ on main):
- **Convex rejects Clerk's DEFAULT token.** The web app uses ConvexProviderWithClerk, which fetches `getToken({template:"convex"})`; the stock clerk-convex-swift provider calls `session.getToken()` with no template, so the audience did not match `applicationID:"convex"` in convex/auth.config.ts and the auth-gated query hung forever (no error, just a spinner). Fix: `HavenConvexAuthProvider` mints the "convex" template token (refresh path re-fetches the templated token too, since Clerk tokens expire ~60s).
- **Clerk iOS needs a keychain entitlement.** Without `keychain-access-groups` it fails with OSStatus -34018 and every sign-in returns 401 "signed out". Fix: `Haven.entitlements` + `CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS` in project.yml. Note: a CLI build with `CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO` strips entitlements and reproduces this; Xcode with a signing team (or ad-hoc `-` signing) applies them. Build/run the sim from CLI with `xcodebuild ... CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY="-" AD_HOC_CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=YES`, then `simctl install`/`launch`/`io ... screenshot`.

Docs on main: mvp-design.md (the plan, stable), todo.md (living backlog/tracker, incl. prototype checkpoints + the iOS App Launch Checklist link), README.md (plain-language intro to Haven, for understanding not contributing).
